items.content:
This Bloomberg chart illustrates the previous comment that higher government bond yields are a global phenomenon.
What makes this cycle different from past ones includes:
G7 Vulnerability: The debt cycle spotlight is as much on G7 economies (France, Japan, and the UK in particular) as on developing countries.
Less Elastic Drivers: The primary catalysts driving yields higher—massive corporate and government supply and, to a lesser extent, oil prices—are less responsive to central bank monetary policy.
Lagged Economic Responses: The repricing out of tech and government bond issuance will lag the damage that higher yields could inflict on traditionally rate-sensitive sectors, including housing, autos, and highly leveraged finance.
 #economy   #markets   #debt   #yields 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 18, 2026

items.title: Olivier’s excellent post below builds on his widely discussed framework of twin debt equilibria dynamics for France and other highly indebted entities. It illustrates how quickly self-reinforcing dynamics can flip: A benign regime of low risk premia and sustainable debt service can rapidly deteriorate following an investor sentiment shift, exogenous shock, etc. This type of regime fragility has been familiar to emerging economies. Increasingly, it is a risk dynamic that is relevant to some advanced economies. #economy #markets #debt @ojblanchard1
items.content:
Olivier’s excellent post below builds on his widely discussed framework of twin debt equilibria dynamics for France and other highly indebted entities.
It illustrates how quickly self-reinforcing dynamics can flip:
A benign regime of low risk premia and sustainable debt service can rapidly deteriorate following an investor sentiment shift, exogenous shock, etc.
This type of regime fragility has been familiar to emerging economies. Increasingly, it is a risk dynamic that is relevant to some advanced economies.
 #economy   #markets   #debt   @ojblanchard1 Olivier Blanchard (@ojblanchard1)Useful to summarize the discussion  about debt and spreads in a graph (based on work with  @pmbruera and  @Gonhuertas . Working paper out soon).

The blue line shows the “good equilibrium” if investors are rationally optimistic. At very low debt, no risk of default, no spread, then a slow increase, and eventually a sudden  jump and default. So, if things get worse (high continuing deficits, increasing debt ratio), reasons to worry.

But, even if things do not get worse, and investors turn (rationally) pessimistic, they require a larger spread, the interest rate jumps and default happens faster. 

I think France is roughly at point A: small spread, but reasons to worry. Deficit is too large, so France keeps moving to the right. And, even if not, equilibrium could jump to point B, with a higher spread.—  https://x.com/ojblanchard1/status/2089626328253214969 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 18, 2026

items.title: Japan’s Q2 GDP Growth Misses Expectations At an annualized rate of 1.1%, Japan's second-quarter GDP growth fell short of both the prior quarter’s 2.1% and the 2.0% consensus forecast. The policy implications of this miss are more consequential given the domestic measures required to support the yen, particularly as the impact of the joint currency intervention continues to erode (please see weekly note). Meanwhile, market pressure remains evident, with 10-year Japanese government bond yields rising to 2.92%, the highest level since 1996. items.title: The always-thoughtful Olivier Blanchard examines the multiple equilibria aspects of France’s fiscal situation. (This analytical framework is also applicable to some other economies.) #economy #markets @ojblanchard1 #debt
items.content:
The always-thoughtful Olivier Blanchard examines the multiple equilibria aspects of France’s fiscal situation.
(This analytical framework is also applicable to some other economies.)
 #economy   #markets   @ojblanchard1   #debt Olivier Blanchard (@ojblanchard1)Many comments on the tweet about the risk of a public debt crisis in France point to the role of the central bank, the ECB in this case, in avoiding multiple equilibria. And, indeed, the ECB has a major role to play.

On paper, it is easy.

There are three zones, determined by fundamentals. At one end, the safe zone: debt is clearly sustainable. At the other end, the default zone: debt is clearly unsustainable. In the middle, the danger zone, where there are multiple equilibria, a good and a bad one., with the bad one leading to a crisis.

If in the safe zone, no need for the central bank to do anything. If in the default zone, need to adjust fiscal policy; not the job of the central bank. If in the danger zone, maintain the good equilibrium, by standing ready to buy if the private investors sell.

This is indeed the mandate of the ECB. If debt is clearly not sustainable, do not intervene unless there is an adjustment program which reestablishes sustainability. If in the danger zone, intervene to keep the interest low and debt sustainable.

In reality, things are not so simple.

When investors require a higher risk premium, how to tell whether we are in the danger zone and the ECB should intervene, or we are already in the default zone, in which case, short an adjustment program, it should not?

The reality: The ECB does not know for sure. And it is likely to be conservative, insist on an adjustment program, with or without a haircut or reprofiling, before intervening. Counting on the ECB to intervene to eliminate multiple equilibria, or even more so, to intervene when debt is clearly unsustainable is unwise.—  https://x.com/ojblanchard1/status/2088595673683722338 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 15, 2026

items.title: Key Takeaways from this morning’s UMich US Consumer Sentiment Survey: The preliminary August consumer sentiment index fell to 51.0 (down from 55.2 in July), well below the consensus forecast of 55.0. Cost-of-living worries contributed to the decline, with survey director Joanne Hsu citing "notably large reductions… among older consumers, lower-income consumers, and those without a college degree." Consistent with the recent rebound in gasoline prices, year-ahead inflation expectations edged higher to 4.3%, while the 5–10 year measure printed at 3.3%. On a positive note, consumer concerns regarding employment remained relatively low. #economy #markets #inflation #employment #affordability
items.content:
Key Takeaways from this morning’s UMich US Consumer Sentiment Survey:
The preliminary August consumer sentiment index fell to 51.0 (down from 55.2 in July), well below the consensus forecast of 55.0.
Cost-of-living worries contributed to the decline, with survey director Joanne Hsu citing "notably large reductions… among older consumers, lower-income consumers, and those without a college degree."
Consistent with the recent rebound in gasoline prices, year-ahead inflation expectations edged higher to 4.3%, while the 5–10 year measure printed at 3.3%.
On a positive note, consumer concerns regarding employment remained relatively low.
 #economy   #markets   #inflation   #employment   #affordability 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 14, 2026
